_about: What PM2.5 and PM10 are and what they do to the body. Limits: CPCB National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) and WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021).

sources.label: CPCB National Ambient Air Quality Standards

particles.title: PM2.5: fine particles
particles.size: 2.5 micrometres or smaller: about 30 times thinner than a human hair. You cannot see one, but together they make the haze.
particles.sources: Vehicle exhaust, burning (crop stubble, rubbish, wood, coal), factories and power plants, firecrackers, and particles that form in the air from gases.
particles.reach_note: Small enough to pass the nose and airways, reach the air sacs deep in the lungs, and the smallest enter the blood.
particles.short_term: Cough, burning eyes and throat, a tight chest and asthma attacks. On bad days more people have heart attacks and strokes.
particles.long_term: Slower lung growth in children, COPD, lung cancer, heart disease, stroke and diabetes, and babies born smaller. It is the air pollutant that shortens lives the most.

particles.title: PM10: coarse dust
particles.size: 10 micrometres or smaller: about 7 times thinner than a hair. It includes all of PM2.5 plus bigger dust.
particles.sources: Road dust, building and demolition work, soil blown by the wind, plus everything in PM2.5.
particles.reach_note: Mostly caught in the nose, throat and upper airways before it reaches the deep lungs.
particles.short_term: Sneezing, a sore throat, coughing and itchy eyes; asthma and bronchitis get worse.
particles.long_term: Breathing it day after day keeps the airways inflamed and worsens asthma and COPD.

protect: A well-fitted N95 (or FFP2) mask filters both; cloth and surgical masks let most PM2.5 through.
Indoors, keep windows shut at the worst hours and air rooms out at the cleanest; a HEPA air purifier cuts indoor PM2.5 sharply.
Skip hard exercise and busy roads when the air is Poor or worse: you breathe in several times more when you exert yourself.
